```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Licensed inputs and individual outputs must never enter a website build.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

An assessment team has several raters score the same essays. It wants to
understand differences in rater severity, inspect ratings that merit discussion,
and consider how many raters to use next time. These are related questions,
but they do not have the same outcome: a many-facet model describes ratings
on a latent scale, whereas a G-Study and D-Study describe error in a specified
observed-score composite.

This worked workflow uses the **human Written ratings in ICNALE GRA v2.1**.
It covers preprocessing, RSM/PCM and GPCM comparisons, local rater feedback,
and planning for a fixed complexity–accuracy–fluency (CAF) composite. It uses the 0.3-series API. Install the package and obtain the workflow
scripts from the **same source checkout** as this article. It is not a complete
reproduction of Yamashita (2024), and it does not evaluate AI ratings.

## Obtain the data yourself

Register with the [official ICNALE download service](https://language.sakura.ne.jp/icnale/download.html)
and obtain the GRA v2.1 workbook under its
[terms of use](https://language.sakura.ne.jp/icnale/index.html).
The corpus, cleaned ratings and individual fitted results are **not distributed
with mfrmr or this website**. Keep your workbook, audit tables, fit objects and
rater sheets in a private directory outside any published repository. Removing
names or saving an RDS file does not turn those objects into redistributable data.
Check the corpus terms before sharing any derived result.

The code below runs on your computer. The website only displays it; neither
pkgdown nor CRAN checks read the workbook or rerun this analysis. Start R in
your matching mfrmr source checkout, with `mfrmr` and `readxl` installed.

```{r input}
library(mfrmr)
source("scripts/icnale-caf/preprocess.R")
source("scripts/icnale-caf/analyse.R")

workbook <- file.choose() # Select ICNALE GRA 2_1.xlsx.
local_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "mfrmr-icnale-local")
dir.create(local_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
input <- read_icnale_caf(workbook)
input$counts
input$category_counts
saveRDS(input, file.path(local_dir, "input.rds"))
```

The reader checks workbook layout, unique rating keys, the essay-rater code
crosswalk and the verification sheet. It stops on a disagreement. Essay ratings
use `W_` identifiers in one sheet and `E_` in another; this crosswalk **does not**
identify spoken raters with the same numerical suffix.

## Define the sample before fitting

The target is **136 L2 writers, 80 raters and three fixed CAF criteria**. Four
English native-speaker benchmark essays are excluded. Every writer produced
one essay on the same topic. The three criteria are not three tasks, and the
data do not separate a writer effect from performance on that single task.

| Quantity | Count |
|:--|--:|
| Candidate writer–rater pairs | 10,880 |
| Pairs excluded by the CAF rule | 118 |
| Retained writer–rater pairs | 10,762 |
| Retained criterion ratings | 32,286 |

Scores must be integers from **0 through 10**; zero is a valid category. For
this subset, a missing, fractional or otherwise invalid score excludes all
three CAF ratings from that writer–rater pair. The source has 161 fractional
CAF scores and one missing CAF score among the candidate pairs; pairwise
exclusion also removes 192 otherwise valid scores. The audit retains both the
original issue and the reason for excluding each cell. No score is rounded,
imputed, or silently collapsed into another category.

This rule makes the three dimensions share the same retained pairs and follows
the selected human CAF subset. It is **a declared analysis choice**, not a
universal cleaning rule for the corpus. Inspect `input$audit` locally. Exclusion
can be informative; preserving a record of it does not establish missingness at
random. The 32,286 ratings are not 32,286 independent writers.

**How large is this design in language-assessment research?** The retained
136 writers and 80 raters form a dense rating design: 10,762 of 10,880 possible
writer–rater pairs remain (98.9%). This should not be described as an
inadequate sample merely because there are fewer writers than ratings.
For context, Nakamura (2002, Research design and method) analysed 32 writers
with four raters, two raters per essay and seven criteria. Schaefer (2008,
§III.3) selected 40 essays from 121 collected essays and had 40 raters assess
them on six criteria. Ahmadi Shirazi (2019, Method) studied 20 writers, each
writing two essays, with eight raters. These are examples of actual research
designs, not a survey establishing a typical sample size or a universal
minimum. The writer count, rater count, crossings, category support and target
precision describe different aspects of a design; none alone supplies a
reason to withhold all intervals. Here we estimate intervals and inspect
their width and model-specific numerical checks.

## Calibrate the ratings and read the numerical review

The RSM uses one shared step structure; the PCM permits a separate step
structure for each criterion. Both models use a single Person dimension,
additive rater severity and criterion difficulty, and unit discrimination.
Rater and criterion locations and each step ladder are centered. An
intercept-only normal Person population has an **estimated mean and SD**;
this is not the package's fixed-standard-normal default.

```{r calibration}
rsm <- icnale_fit(input, "RSM", local_dir)
pcm <- icnale_fit(input, "PCM", local_dir)
summary(rsm, compute = "never")
summary(pcm, compute = "never")
rsm$data_review$category_support
pcm$data_review$category_support
```

`icnale_fit()` calls `fit_mfrm()` with explicit `spec` and `control` lists;
read `scripts/icnale-caf/analyse.R` to see or adapt those choices. It uses
accuracy-controlled direct MML: the retained rule is checked against finer
adaptive integration for likelihood, posterior moments and gradients. If the
criteria fail, it saves the failure locally and stops without returning a fit.
Do not interpret an optimizer's zero convergence code alone as numerical
adequacy. Stored fits are reused only when the input, model, controls and
installed package code match; use a new output directory after changing them.

Sparse categories within individual raters remain visible in the category
review even though the full data contain all eleven categories. A numerical
pass does not remove a category warning or certify the sampling properties of
an interval. Read the fit's review together with the result-specific checks.

CAF can have different substantive meanings and residual associations. Better
fit of the PCM would describe the benefit of separate step structures within
this model family; it would not prove a single CAF ability dimension or local
independence. One corpus cannot establish the model's coverage across sample
sizes or assessment settings.

## Review a rater locally

Choose a rater identifier from your own data after inspecting the whole fit.
The first identifier below is only an example of selecting a sheet, not a
data-driven flag for poor performance.

```{r feedback}
chosen_rater <- sort(unique(input$ratings$Rater))[1]
feedback <- icnale_feedback(rsm, local_dir, rater = chosen_rater)
summary(feedback$results)
browseURL(file.path(local_dir, "rater-sheet.html"))
```

The sheet combines the fitted severity, available uncertainty and diagnostics.
Positive severity means lower expected ratings, conditional on the fitted
writer and criterion effects. A difference from zero is relative to the
centering constraint, not an external standard of correct scoring. An interval
or fit statistic does not establish unfairness or rater incompetence. Keep
unavailable uncertainty and its reason visible; do not replace it with zero.
Use the sheet to select concrete rubric and scoring questions for discussion.
The example suppresses individual rating cases in the HTML with `max_cases = 0`;
the local result objects still contain data and must remain private.

**What happened in this example:** both calibrations passed their integration
and stationarity criteria, and both provide pointwise 95% Wald intervals for
all 80 rater severities. RSM SEs range from 0.0253 to 0.0348 native logits;
PCM SEs are almost the same. Each interval uses the full joint marginal
information, including uncertainty in the estimated normal population.
All eleven categories are supported in each fitted step scope. An individual
rater need not use every category of the shared RSM step ladder. Sparse local
counts remain visible as a diagnostic, rather than automatically disqualifying
every interval. Inspect both the interval table and its numerical checks:

```{r interval-status}
feedback$results$facet_intervals$raters$checks
table(feedback$results$facet_intervals$raters$table$Status)
```

The RSM's full covariance is stable when adaptive integration increases from
31 to 61 points (standardized matrix change below `2e-12`). This establishes
numerical stability for the fitted model, not empirical coverage of 95%.
The intervals assume the declared model and conditional independence; they
do not cover arbitrary rater-by-writer dependence or generalization to new
tasks. Do not change models just to obtain intervals or replace missing
bounds with zero.

## Compare PCM and one- or two-family GPCM

These are different response models, not four different estimation methods.
First hold the estimation method (MML), retained ratings and normal population
family constant. For score `k`, the adjacent-category log odds are
`a[c] * b[r] * (theta[p] - severity[r] - difficulty[c] - step[c,k])`.
RSM and PCM fix both slopes to one; RSM additionally shares its step ladder
across criteria. The one-family GPCM estimates criterion slopes `a[c]`.
The two-family GPCM also estimates rater slopes `b[r]`. This full-predictor
product model must not be confused with every model called a rater GPCM.

```{r gpcm-calibration}
gpcm1 <- icnale_fit(input, "GPCM1", local_dir)
gpcm2 <- icnale_fit(input, "GPCM2", local_dir)
fits <- list(RSM = rsm, PCM = pcm, GPCM1 = gpcm1, GPCM2 = gpcm2)
summary(gpcm1, compute = "never")
summary(gpcm2, compute = "never")
```

The one-family model centers the relative criterion slopes at geometric mean
one and estimates the normal population mean/SD. The two-family model fixes
the population to N(0,1), centers the criterion slope family at geometric mean
one, leaves rater slopes free, and places the location origin in Criterion.
This allocates the overall unit to the rater slope family instead of the
population SD. Raw coefficients across these parameterizations are not directly
comparable. In particular, a two-family rater slope below one is not itself
evidence of poor consistency relative to another model's unit slope.

| Model | Free parameters | Marginal log likelihood |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| RSM | 92 | -66,174.3655 |
| PCM | 110 | -66,133.3957 |
| Criterion-slope GPCM | 112 | -66,129.1013 |
| Criterion-by-rater-slope GPCM | 191 | -64,677.0617 |

All four fits pass their numerical point-estimation criteria. The two-family
fit also reaches the same likelihood from retained and perturbed starting
coordinates. This is evidence about these numerical solutions, not proof of a
global maximum or out-of-sample superiority. Adding 79 rater-slope coordinates
improves the in-sample likelihood substantially; it also allows the model to
absorb differences previously visible as rater misfit. Do not select a model
solely because its Pathway points move toward one.

### Compare locations, category boundaries and Pathway plots

```{r model-comparison-plots}
source("scripts/icnale-caf/compare.R")
comparison <- icnale_comparison_plots(fits)
comparison$plots$wright
comparison$plots$thresholds
comparison$plots$pathway
comparison$plots$expected
saveRDS(comparison, file.path(local_dir, "model-comparison.rds"))
```

These are local workflow figures, with their numerical tables saved alongside
them. The Wright-type location display uses `z = (theta - mu) / sigma`.
Rater offsets are divided by `sigma`; the origin shift is assigned to
Criterion, whose locations become `(difficulty - mu) / sigma`. Step offsets
are divided by `sigma`. Subtracting `mu` separately from every facet would
change the predictor. The boundary plot shows adjacent-category equality
points at zero rater location, not Thurstonian cumulative-probability
thresholds. The expected-score plot averages equally across the same 80
raters at each standardized ability and criterion.

The Pathway-type plot puts conditional EAP plug-in Infit MnSq on the horizontal
axis and standardized rater location vertically. Its numerator is the sum
of squared residuals; its denominator is the sum of conditional rating
variances. Both are recalculated under each fitted response model. It is a
descriptive comparison without a calibrated acceptance band, ZSTD test or
automatic rater classification. In particular it is not a posterior-predictive
residual summary. The ordinary `plot(fit, type = "fit_pathway")` and
`plot(fit, type = "wright")` routes retain their documented support; this
workflow does not silently make those methods available for two-family GPCM.
`type = "pathway"` in the ordinary API instead draws expected-score pathways.

In this example, standardized rater locations barely change from RSM to PCM
(maximum change 0.00059 population SD), change by at most 0.0196 under the
criterion-slope GPCM, and by at most 0.304 under the two-family GPCM. Person
EAP correlations with RSM are above 0.99999 for PCM and one-family GPCM and
0.9956 for two-family GPCM. Rater Infit spans approximately 0.51–2.01 in the
first three models and 0.78–1.31 in the two-family model. These results locate
the practical change in this dataset: allowing different rater slopes matters
more than allowing different criterion slopes. They do not establish which
model measures the intended construct best.

Keep native-scale interval plots separate from this point comparison:

```{r model-intervals}
ci_rsm <- feedback$results$facet_intervals$raters # Reuse the qualified result.
ci_pcm <- mfrm_facet_intervals(pcm, "Rater")
ci_gpcm1 <- mfrm_facet_intervals(gpcm1, "Rater")
ci_gpcm2 <- mfrm_facet_intervals(gpcm2, "Rater")
plot(ci_rsm)
plot(ci_pcm)
plot(ci_gpcm1)
plot(ci_gpcm2)
saveRDS(list(RSM = ci_rsm, PCM = ci_pcm, GPCM1 = ci_gpcm1, GPCM2 = ci_gpcm2),
  file.path(local_dir, "rater-intervals.rds"))
```

All 80 location intervals are available for each of these four fits after
their model-specific checks. Simply dividing interval endpoints by an
estimated SD would omit that SD's uncertainty. Use the supported standardized
interval API when that is the inferential target; the workflow's location
figures deliberately display points without implying transformed confidence
intervals. The two-family results retain their experimental qualification and
saved diagnostics. In this fit, all 83 component
slope intervals pass the local numerical checks. The observed Person-score
rank is 135 for 191 free parameters: a full-parameter empirical sandwich
covariance is unavailable, but the full observed Hessian is positive definite.
The model-based intervals use that observed information; a rule requiring
more writers than free parameters would incorrectly conflate the two
information matrices. This does not establish robustness to model
misspecification or finite-sample coverage.

## A bounded comparison with TAM

The RSM was also checked with TAM 4.3-25 using the same retained CAF pairs,
`formulaA = ~ item + rater + step`, and `constraint = "cases"`. Crucially,
`pid = input$wide$Person` keeps repeated rows within the same writer; omitting
it changes the model to one Person per writer–rater row. Both models estimate
normal population variance. TAM fixes the population mean at zero and leaves
the mean criterion location free; the mfrmr parameterization above centers
criterion locations and estimates the population mean. Compare centered
criterion locations and the corresponding shifted population origin.

After convergence, refining TAM's grid over [-6, 6] from 481 to 961 points
changed its log likelihood by less than 10^-9. Against mfrmr's adaptive result,
the absolute log-likelihood difference was below 10^-8, and the largest
differences in rater locations and centered steps were below 10^-6. This is
an implementation check for **RSM point estimates in this dataset**, not a
comparison of interval coverage, a PCM cross-check, or a validation of the
single-dimension model. Equal node counts alone are not an accuracy match.
TAM's initial unaccelerated fit reached its iteration limit; only the
converged continuation and finer-grid results were used in this comparison.

To set up your own comparison, the essential call is below. Follow the
[TAM manual](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/TAM/TAM.pdf) to inspect
convergence and repeat with a finer grid before interpreting differences.
Keep these data-bearing objects local too.

```{r tam-setup}
tam <- TAM::tam.mml.mfr(
  resp = as.matrix(input$wide[c("Complexity", "Accuracy", "Fluency")]),
  facets = data.frame(rater = input$wide$Rater),
  pid = input$wide$Person,
  formulaA = ~ item + rater + step, constraint = "cases",
  control = list(nodes = seq(-6, 6, length.out = 241), snodes = 0,
    xsi.start0 = TRUE, maxiter = 1000, conv = 1e-8, convD = 1e-8,
    convM = 1e-8, progress = FALSE), verbose = FALSE
)
tam$iter # Reaching maxiter is not evidence of convergence.

# Continue from the saved candidate, then refine the grid. Each result must
# converge; an iteration limit never counts as a successful comparison.
for (points in c(241L, 481L, 961L)) {
  previous <- tam
  tam <- TAM::tam.mml.mfr(
    resp = as.matrix(input$wide[c("Complexity", "Accuracy", "Fluency")]),
    facets = data.frame(rater = input$wide$Rater), pid = input$wide$Person,
    formulaA = ~ item + rater + step, constraint = "cases",
    xsi.inits = cbind(seq_len(nrow(previous$xsi)), previous$xsi$xsi),
    variance.inits = previous$variance,
    control = list(nodes = seq(-6, 6, length.out = points), snodes = 0,
      acceleration = "Ramsay", maxiter = 1000, conv = 1e-8, convD = 1e-8,
      convM = 1e-8, progress = FALSE), verbose = FALSE
  )
  stopifnot(tam$iter < 1000)
}
c(logLik_change = abs(tam$deviance - previous$deviance) / 2,
  parameter_change = max(abs(tam$xsi$xsi - previous$xsi$xsi)))
saveRDS(tam, file.path(local_dir, "tam-rsm.rds"))
```

## A bounded comparison with ConQuest

The local comparison uses **ConQuest 5.47.5, Standard Version**. The
[Standard licence](https://vpol.acer.edu.au/au/conquest/conquest-faq) permits
100 items. In this wide-format design each rater–criterion combination is a
generalized item, so the complete 80 × 3 design has 240 items. We therefore
compare a declared subset of 32 raters, selected by evenly spaced positions
in the sorted identifier list before estimation. Both programs use the same
136 writers and 12,813 retained ratings. This is a software comparison on
a subset, not a replacement for the full-sample analysis or a random sample
of the rater population.

```{r conquest-export}
source("scripts/icnale-caf/conquest.R")
raters <- sort(unique(input$ratings$Rater))[
  unique(round(seq(1, 80, length.out = 32)))]
conquest_dir <- file.path(local_dir, "conquest-comparison")
manifest <- icnale_conquest(input, raters, conquest_dir)

subset_input <- input
subset_input$ratings <- input$ratings[input$ratings$Rater %in% raters, ]
subset_rsm <- icnale_fit(subset_input, "RSM", conquest_dir)
subset_pcm <- icnale_fit(subset_input, "PCM", conquest_dir)
```

Open ConQuest in that local output directory and submit `rsm.cqc`, then
`pcm.cqc`. On a Mac with the default installation, the executable is
`/Applications/ConQuest/ConQuest`. Use a fresh directory for another run;
existing output files trigger interactive overwrite prompts. The generated
models are `criteria + rater + step` for RSM and
`criteria + rater + criteria*step` for PCM. Each writer occupies one physical
record with 96 response columns, preserving one ability per writer.

The exporter preserves the declared **0–10 category ladder for every
generalized item**. It appends 11 support records with weight exactly zero
and uses `skipwtzero=no`; real writer records have weight one. These support
records contribute zero to the marginal log likelihood. ConQuest nevertheless
includes them in some displayed case counts. Do not interpret those counts,
its printed BIC or fit summaries as results for additional writers. This
comparison uses the actual 136 writers, the marginal likelihood, aligned
coefficients and model-based SEs. See the
[command reference](https://conquestmanual.acer.org/s4-00.html) for `caseweight`,
`score`, `skipwtzero` and `estimate`.

Both programs estimate the normal population variance. ConQuest fixes its
mean to zero and leaves the criterion origin free. To align it with the
native fit, retain the centered rater locations and step offsets and compare
ConQuest criterion locations with `native difficulty - native population mean`.
Refine the exported 481-point grid over [-6, 6] to 961 points after convergence,
using the exported parameter and population-variance files as starts. The
finer point-estimate run can use `stderr=none, fit=no`; the earlier SE results
remain separate evidence. An iteration limit is not a convergence certificate.

For both RSM and PCM, the aligned location and step differences are below
`1e-5`; all 32 rater SE differences are below `0.0005`, half the rounding unit of the printed
three-decimal SEs. The finer grid preserves the reported deviance. These are
implementation comparisons at the available output precision, not evidence
that either program's intervals attain nominal coverage. ConQuest's ordinary
GPCM with a free slope per generalized item is not the same restriction as
the criterion-by-rater product slope model above, and is not reported as a
like-for-like two-family comparison.

## Plan ratings for a fixed observed-score composite

Now change the question: how variable would the **equal-weight average of
the three CAF scores** be under a specified future rater design? This uses
the original 0–10 observed scores, not model-adjusted abilities or MML posterior
SDs. CAF are fixed score dimensions; Rater is the one random facet. The
multivariate MINQUE(0) G-Study allows the incomplete retained Person × Rater
table and estimates covariances between the dimensions.

```{r planning}
planning <- icnale_planning(input)
summary(planning$g)
summary(planning$d)
plot(planning$d)
saveRDS(planning, file.path(local_dir, "planning.rds"))
```

The D-Study considers 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 **common random raters** for every
writer and all three scores, with equal weights of 1/3. It projects complete
balanced future designs; it does not reproduce the missing assignments in
the source data. `G` concerns relative comparisons among writers; `Phi` also
counts rater-level shifts as error for absolute decisions. SEM stays on the
observed composite scale. In the checked v2.1 subset the equal-weight composite
gives these point projections (rounded):

| Common raters | G | Phi | Absolute SEM |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 0.308 | 0.298 | 1.810 |
| 2 | 0.471 | 0.459 | 1.280 |
| 3 | 0.571 | 0.560 | 1.045 |
| 4 | 0.640 | 0.629 | 0.905 |
| 6 | 0.727 | 0.718 | 0.739 |
| 8 | 0.781 | 0.773 | 0.640 |

These numbers show the modeled improvement as rater replication increases,
not an empirically validated guarantee for a new assessment. The projections condition on estimated covariance
components and supply no confidence intervals here. They are not a guaranteed
minimum-rater recommendation, and they do not cover independent rater panels
for different writers or a new population of tasks.

## Save and return in a new R session

```{r reload}
library(mfrmr)
local_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "mfrmr-icnale-local")
rsm <- readRDS(file.path(local_dir, "rsm-fit.rds"))$fit
results <- readRDS(file.path(local_dir, "results.rds"))
planning <- readRDS(file.path(local_dir, "planning.rds"))
summary(rsm, compute = "never")
summary(results)
summary(planning$d)
```

Keep the source checkout, R/package versions and workbook version with your
local analysis. The saved-fit bundle records settings, input identity and
session information. Reloading preserves an analysis; it does not upgrade
the evidence or make private data public.

## What this example can and cannot establish

Ishikawa (2024, §§2.1–2.2) describes the task and the rating instructions.
Raters were instructed to aim for analytic score means of 4–6 and SDs of 2–3
on the ten-point range. Those are instructions, not evidence that every rater
complied. The observed spread and severity are therefore not an unrestricted
sample of ordinary classroom rating behavior. Language-background contrasts,
causal training effects, population-wide fairness, and generalization over new
tasks require their own designs. Do not mistake rater demographic variables
for writer demographics.

The value of this example is a traceable route from licensed source ratings
to explicit analysis choices, diagnostics and a conditional assessment plan.
Synthetic simulations remain necessary for claims about bias, interval
coverage or minimum sample sizes, because the true abilities and severities
are unknown in these data.

- Ishikawa, S. (2024). The ICNALE Global Rating Archives: A New Assessment
  Dataset for Learner Corpus Studies. *Learner Corpus Studies in Asia and
  the World*, 6, 13–38.
  See the [version of record](https://da.lib.kobe-u.ac.jp/da/kernel/0100487713/0100487713.pdf),
  especially §§2.1–2.4, for tasks, ratings and raters.
- Yamashita (2024), [article DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rmal.2024.100133).
  This example isolates human CAF ratings; it does not reproduce the full
  study or its AI comparisons.
- Nakamura, Y. (2002). [An application of a many-faceted Rasch model to
  writing test analysis (Part 1)](https://pansig.org/publications/pansig/2002/HTML/Nakamura.htm).
  See Research design and method and the category SEs in Table 1.
- Schaefer, E. (2008). [Rater bias patterns in an EFL writing
  assessment](https://doi.org/10.1177/0265532208094273). *Language Testing*.
  The data-collection section distinguishes the 121 collected essays from
  the 40 actually rated.
- Ahmadi Shirazi, M. (2019). [For a Greater Good: Bias Analysis in Writing
  Assessment](https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244018822377). *SAGE Open*.
  Method distinguishes 20 writers from their 40 essays.
- [ICNALE corpus modules](https://language.sakura.ne.jp/icnale/modules.html),
